archetypes.name: Bowtie antenna
archetypes.summary: Planar triangular dipole; the flat approximation to a biconical antenna.

synthesis.notes: each half is about a quarter wave at the low-frequency edge

analysis.notes: Mushiake's relation: a self-complementary planar structure in an infinite zero-thickness sheet has Zin = eta0/2 = 188.37 ohm, INDEPENDENT of frequency and of the flare angle. A bowtie is self-complementary only at a 90 degree flare. Solved, this spec's finite 90-degree bowtie reaches it only once its wings are several half-wavelengths long: from 2.5 f_low its input impedance ripples between 166 and 216 ohm (mean 198) with under 41 ohm of reactance.
1 when the flare is 90 degrees, where the metal and air regions are congruent

SOLVED by the planar method of moments (otahub.num.rwg: triangles and RWG functions, checked against the rooftop strip solver to 0.04-0.2% in resistance and against the wire MoM): broadside directivity at f_low, each wing a quarter wavelength, over flares 30-90 degrees - 2.30 to 2.53 dBi. The 2.3 dBi this spec carried as indicative holds at f_low for narrow flares, but not 'fairly flat with frequency': at 90 degrees broadside climbs to 3.5 dBi at 1.75 f_low, then the beam splits - -3.7 dBi broadside at 3 f_low and -19 at 3.5, the peak moving off axis. A 75-degree bowtie solved directly lands within 0.02% of the interpolation. NaN outside 30-90 degrees (at 120 the wide wings drop it to 1.65 dBi).

Indicative, and conservative against a 188 ohm reference: solved, the 90-degree bowtie stays below VSWR 2 against eta0/2 from f_low to 4 f_low, the top of the solved range; where it ends above that was not solved. The infinite structure would be frequency independent; the wings' truncation sets the low end.

SOLVED (rwg) at f_low, fed across a gap a hundredth of a wavelength wide at the apex: 148 ohm at 30 degrees to 208 at 90 - not Mushiake's 188, which is the infinite sheet's. A 75-degree bowtie solved directly lands within 1.4% of the interpolation. NaN outside 30-90 degrees.
+135 to +186 ohm at f_low: the finite bowtie is inductive there and first resonates near 1.3 f_low (90 degrees, about 305 ohm). The 75-degree solve lands within 0.5% of the interpolation.

validity: Mushiake's impedance assumes an INFINITE, zero-thickness, perfectly conducting self-complementary sheet. A real bowtie is finite and printed on a substrate, so measured impedance typically lands well below 188 ohm.
a substrate shifts the impedance down by roughly sqrt(eps_reff)
directivity and the f_low impedance are solved for a free-standing zero-thickness sheet, flares 30-90 degrees, fed at the apex across a gap of 0.01 lambda_low; the bandwidth ratio stays indicative

known_cases.source: Mushiake: Zin = eta0/2 = 188.365 ohm for the 90 degree self-complementary bowtie. Quarter wave at 1 GHz = 74.95 mm. Mushiake, Self-Complementary Antennas, IEEE AP Magazine 34(6), 1992
A 60 degree flare is not self-complementary, so Mushiake's relation does not apply. Mushiake, Self-Complementary Antennas, IEEE AP Magazine 34(6), 1992
A 75-degree bowtie solved directly by otahub.num.rwg (40 x 16 cells a wing, not the interpolation): at f_low.

references: Mushiake, Self-Complementary Antennas, IEEE AP Magazine 34(6), 1992
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 11
Schantz, The Art and Science of Ultra-Wideband Antennas, Artech House

archetypes.name: Planar circular disc monopole
archetypes.summary: Circular disc fed against a ground plane; a common printed UWB radiator.

synthesis.notes: Inverts the standard empirical rule f_low[GHz] = 7.2/(L + r + p) with lengths in cm, where for a disc the effective height L = 2*r. In SI this reads f_low = 7.2e7/(2r + r + p), hence r = (7.2e7/f_low - p)/3. EMPIRICAL, roughly 10% accurate.

analysis.notes: forward check of the empirical rule; must return f_low
the disc is modelled as an equivalent cylindrical monopole of this height, which is where the empirical rule comes from
Indicative: disc monopoles routinely cover 10:1 for VSWR < 2, limited at the top by the feed transition rather than the disc
Indicative: roughly monopole-like at the low end, becoming more directive and less predictable as higher-order modes appear

validity: EMPIRICAL rule, roughly 10% accurate on f_low; always verify in a solver
assumes a ground plane at least a quarter wave across at f_low
the pattern degrades badly at the top of the band as the disc becomes several wavelengths across - bandwidth here means impedance bandwidth, not pattern bandwidth
bandwidth and directivity entries are indicative

known_cases.source: f_low = 3 GHz with a 1 mm feed gap gives r = (24.0 - 1.0)/3 = 7.67 mm by the 7.2/(L+r+p) rule. Ammann & Chen, Wideband monopole antennas for multi-band wireless systems, IEEE AP Magazine 45(2), 2003
Scaling check: 1 GHz needs r = (72.0 - 1.0)/3 = 23.67 mm.

references: Ammann & Chen, Wideband monopole antennas for multi-band wireless systems, IEEE AP Magazine 45(2), 2003
Schantz, The Art and Science of Ultra-Wideband Antennas, Artech House

archetypes.name: Archimedean spiral
archetypes.summary: Two-arm spiral with linear radial growth; circularly polarised over a wide band.

synthesis.notes: The active region is the ring whose circumference is one wavelength, so the lowest frequency is set by the OUTER circumference: 2*pi*r_out = lambda_low.
the highest frequency is set by the innermost circumference at the feed
r = r_in + growth*phi; the growth rate follows from spanning r_in to r_out in n_turns revolutions

analysis.notes: Mushiake again: a self-complementary two-arm spiral (equal metal and gap widths) presents eta0/2 = 188.37 ohm. Needs a balun and a taper to reach 50 ohm. Solved, the finite spiral's input depends on its feed region, which this spec does not describe: with a small bridge across the centre the equiangular spiral read 154 - j67 ohm at 2.5 f_low on a 10:1 design and 188 - j43 on a 20:1 one, whose only difference is the inner radius, while its axial ratio moved 0.15 dB and its directivity 0.1%. Mushiake's figure is the infinite sheet's.

SOLVED by the planar method of moments (otahub.num.rwg) for six turns and a 10:1 band: broadside directivity at 3 f_low, the band's geometric middle - 5.46 dBi per side, not the 1.8 dBi (1.5) this spec carried. It rises across the band: 3.5 at 1, 3.9 at 1.5, 4.3 at 2, 5.5 at 3, 6.1 at 4 f_low (dBi). NaN for geometries not solved.

Backing the spiral with an absorber-loaded cavity makes it unidirectional but absorbs half the power, so the net gain is roughly unchanged from bidirectional. A resonant cavity does better but only over a narrow band. Do NOT assume 3 dB free. Now built on the solved free-space directivity; the absorber cavity itself stays INDICATIVE.
SOLVED (rwg), on boresight at 3 f_low: 0.68 dB. It is 16 dB at f_low itself and falls through 3 dB at 1.33 f_low (cp_band_low_edge_over_f_low).

SOLVED (rwg, a bisection of direct solves): the frequency, in units of f_low, where the boresight axial ratio falls through 3 dB - 1.331. This spec sets f_low where the outer circumference is one wavelength; there the axial ratio is 16 dB, so the circularly polarised band starts 33% higher. Size the outer radius for this edge, not for f_low, when circular polarisation is the requirement.

validity: the spiral must have enough turns for the active region to form: n_turns >= 3
truncation at r_out causes reflection from the open end, which is the main source of axial-ratio degradation at the low edge
radiates bidirectionally; a cavity costs roughly 3 dB unless it is resonant
directivity, axial ratio and the circular-polarisation band edge are solved (otahub.num.rwg) for a free-standing zero-thickness spiral with six turns and a 10:1 band; NaN otherwise

known_cases.source: 2*pi*r_out = lambda at 1 GHz gives r_out = 47.71 mm; the 10 GHz inner radius is one tenth of it. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 11
Self-complementary two-arm spiral: eta0/2. Mushiake, Self-Complementary Antennas, IEEE AP Magazine 34(6), 1992
otahub.num.rwg solved directly: the 3 dB axial-ratio crossing by bisection of solves (1.3313 f_low) and the broadside directivity at 3 f_low.

references: Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 11 (11.3)
Rumsey, Frequency Independent Antennas, Academic Press 1966
Mushiake, Self-Complementary Antennas, IEEE AP Magazine 34(6), 1992

archetypes.name: Equiangular (log-spiral) antenna
archetypes.summary: Exponentially growing two-arm spiral; shape defined by angles alone, so truly frequency independent.

analysis.notes: r = r0*exp(a*phi), so spanning the band needs phi = ln(r_out/r0)/a radians
the radius multiplier per revolution; 4 is a common choice (a = 0.221)

self-complementary case; Mushiake's relation Solved, the finite spiral's input depends on its feed region, which this spec does not describe: with a small bridge across the centre the equiangular spiral read 154 - j67 ohm at 2.5 f_low on a 10:1 design and 188 - j43 on a 20:1 one, whose only difference is the inner radius, while its axial ratio moved 0.15 dB and its directivity 0.1%. Mushiake's figure is the infinite sheet's.

SOLVED by the planar method of moments (otahub.num.rwg) for a = 0.221 and a 10:1 to 20:1 band: broadside directivity at 3 f_low, the band's geometric middle - 5.24 dBi per side, not the 1.8 dBi (1.5) this spec carried. It rises across the band: 2.7 at 1, 3.6 at 1.5, 4.2 at 2, 5.2 at 3, 6.0 at 4 f_low (dBi). NaN for geometries not solved.

SOLVED (rwg, a bisection of direct solves): the frequency, in units of f_low, where the boresight axial ratio falls through 3 dB - 2.285. This spec sets f_low where the outer circumference is one wavelength; there the axial ratio is 21 dB, so the circularly polarised band starts 129% higher. Size the outer radius for this edge, not for f_low, when circular polarisation is the requirement.

validity: the defining property is that the shape is specified entirely by angles, so performance is frequency independent only where the structure is untruncated
both band edges come from truncation: the outer radius at the low end, the feed region at the high end
self-complementary impedance requires equal arm and gap angular widths
directivity, axial ratio and the circular-polarisation band edge are solved (otahub.num.rwg) for a free-standing zero-thickness spiral with a = 0.221 and a 10:1 to 20:1 band; NaN otherwise

known_cases.source: a = 0.221 gives exp(2*pi*0.221) = 4.007, i.e. the radius quadruples per turn, so a decade needs ln(10)/(2*pi*0.221) = 1.66 turns. Rumsey, Frequency Independent Antennas, Academic Press 1966
Mushiake, Self-Complementary Antennas, IEEE AP Magazine 34(6), 1992
otahub.num.rwg solved directly: the 3 dB axial-ratio crossing by bisection of solves (2.2855 f_low) and the broadside directivity at 3 f_low.

references: Rumsey, Frequency Independent Antennas, Academic Press 1966
Dyson, The Equiangular Spiral Antenna, IRE Trans. AP-7, 1959
Mushiake, Self-Complementary Antennas, IEEE AP Magazine 34(6), 1992

archetypes.name: Vivaldi (exponentially tapered slot) antenna
archetypes.summary: Exponentially flared slot in a ground plane; endfire, wideband, linearly polarised.

synthesis.notes: The low-frequency limit is set by the APERTURE WIDTH reaching about half a wavelength, not by the taper rate or the axial length.

analysis.notes: should be 0.5 by construction
Gain grows with axial length in wavelengths; below about 1 the antenna is not really endfire
APPROXIMATE endfire scaling G ~ 10*(L/lambda), the standard travelling-wave estimate. Real Vivaldis run 5-12 dBi and the figure rises across the band because L/lambda does. Expect 2 dB error.
y = C1*exp(R*z) + C2; this is the growth factor over the full axial length
Indicative: the top of the band is set by the feed transition (microstrip-to-slotline or antipodal), not by the taper. Well-made Vivaldis exceed 10:1.

validity: low-frequency edge is set by aperture width; a longer taper does NOT lower it
high-frequency edge is set by the feed transition, which is not modelled here
gain expression is an approximate endfire scaling, roughly 2 dB accurate, and is frequency dependent since L/lambda varies across the band
substrate thickness must stay well below lambda/4 at the top of the band or surface-wave loss dominates

known_cases.source: Aperture = lambda/2 at 1 GHz = 149.9 mm; a 0.3 m axial length is almost exactly one wavelength. Gibson, The Vivaldi Aerial, 9th European Microwave Conf., 1979
Doubling the axial length to 2 lambda gives roughly 3 dB more by the endfire scaling G ~ 10*(L/lambda).

references: Gibson, The Vivaldi Aerial, 9th European Microwave Conf., 1979
Schantz, The Art and Science of Ultra-Wideband Antennas, Artech House

archetypes.name: Discone
archetypes.summary: Cone against a disc, fed at the apex: an omnidirectional wideband antenna whose low cutoff, 50 ohm bandwidth and gain are solved here as a body of revolution rather than taken from rules of thumb.

parameters.name: slant length at f_low, in wavelengths

synthesis.notes: SOLVED, then tabulated: the slant (from the ideal apex) at which VSWR in 50 ohm first falls to 2, found by otahub.num.bor - the exact axisymmetric surface problem, solid cone and disc, the finite feed below - on meshes of 24 and 48 segments per slant, extrapolated (the 48-segment answer is within 0.4% of the limit). Bilinear in half angle (20-50 deg, 5 deg steps) and disc ratio (0.6-0.9); 0.9% worst on 6 held-out designs between the grid points. The quarter-wave rule this replaces falls 3-23% short at 20-35 degrees and 33-58% short at 45-50, 12% at the default - wider cones start working later, not earlier. The survey left the two free edges - the cone's base rim and the disc's rim - on uniform segments, where the current is edge-singular; rebuilt with both graded, the extrapolated cutoff lands within 0.05% of this table at six designs.
About 0.7 of the cone base is the long-standing rule; the disc is the second half of the bicone, flattened

The feed: the cone is truncated where the coax shield meets it, at 2% of the base diameter - an N-type connector's size on a VHF discone. It is part of the design, not a detail: the solved cutoff moves up 1.3-1.8% for each further 1% of the base diameter at 20-30 degrees (hardly at all at 45), and the proportion this spec used to imply, a top a third of the base RADIUS, moved it up 23% and cut a 30 degree discone's band to 4.8:1.
Spacing S between the cone's top face and the disc, Nail's S = 0.3 x top diameter.
height of the truncated cone, top face to base; the slant is measured from the ideal apex

analysis.notes: What a full bicone of this half angle would present. The discone is roughly half a bicone, but the flat disc perturbs it toward 50 ohm - which is why the geometry is used at all.
the same cone over an INFINITE ground plane: exactly half the biconical value
forward check: must return f_low

SOLVED, tabulated: f_high/f_low for the CONTINUOUS band with VSWR under 2 in 50 ohm above the low cutoff. At least a decade (the table's 10: VSWR under 2 all the way to 10 f_low, the end of the survey) for every cone of 30 degrees or more at every disc ratio, and at 25 degrees with a 0.6 disc; 3.1:1 to 5.1:1 for the narrower cones. So the decade this spec asserted as indicative is right for the default 30 degree cone and wider ones - with a coax-sized feed - and wrong for narrow cones, whose VSWR climbs back past 2 within the decade. Where a ripple touches 2 the band edge can jump between grid points, which the table interpolates across.
bandwidth_ratio times f_low. Where the table reads 10 the survey stopped at 10 f_low with VSWR still under 2, so this is a lower bound there.

SOLVED, tabulated: the highest VSWR in 50 ohm between 2 f_low and 10 f_low, once the low-frequency roll-off is behind - the margin inside the band. It is 1.86 at the default; 1.48-2.00 across the cones that hold the decade, and 2.07-2.41 on the 20-25 degree cones that do not. At 30 degrees with a 0.9 disc, and at 25 with 0.6, the peak sits at 2.00 within the mesh's resolution (1.995-2.004 over meshes and frequency grids, graded edges or not): there the decade is marginal, and any real feed will decide it.

SOLVED, tabulated: peak directivity at f_low from the solved currents' far field. 1.24 to 1.54 linear across the box, 1.482 (1.71 dBi) at the default. The previous flat 2.2 (3.4 dBi) was 48% high. It rises across the band as the beam tilts downward: at the default, 2.35 with the peak 50 degrees below the horizon at 3 f_low, 4.00 at 70 degrees at 6 f_low.
vertical, as for any monopole-like radiator

validity: solved for 20 <= half angle <= 50 degrees and 0.6 <= disc ratio <= 0.9 with the feed stated here (top diameter 2% of the base, S = 0.3 x top diameter); outside that box the tables clamp

solid, perfectly conducting cone and zero-thickness disc on a common axis, and an infinitesimally thin feed gap region carrying a uniform field - a real coax transition, a thick disc or a wire-spoke cone will differ, most at the top of the band
free space: no mast, no ground below the cone
50 ohm reference for every VSWR quoted
the elevation pattern tilts progressively downward with frequency; only the azimuth pattern is broadband

known_cases.source: Default discone at 100 MHz: the body-of-revolution solve puts VSWR = 2 in 50 ohm at a slant of 0.2801 wavelengths (0.2821 on 24 and 0.2811 on 48 segments per slant, extrapolated), 839.7 mm - 12.0% longer than the quarter wave this spec used, 749.5 mm.

Same design: VSWR stays under 2 from f_low right through 10 f_low, so the decade this spec asserted as indicative is real for it - with a coax-sized feed. Its worst VSWR between 2 and 10 f_low is 1.865.
A narrow cone, 20 degrees: the band under VSWR 2 ends at 4.80 f_low and the VSWR reaches 2.30 before 10 f_low. The decade is a property of cones of 30 degrees or more.
Peak directivity at f_low from the solved far field: 1.482, 1.71 dBi, against the flat 2.2 (3.42 dBi) asserted before.

A wide cone, 50 degrees with a 0.6 disc: its VSWR reaches 2 only at a slant of 0.3949 wavelengths, 58% longer than a quarter wave - a wider cone matches 50 ohm better once it is working, and starts working later.
Between the table's grid points (32.5 degrees, 0.75): solved directly, low cutoff at 0.2800 wavelengths; the bilinear table gives 0.2819.
Unchanged reference values: eta0/pi * ln(cot(15 deg)) = 157.93 ohm for a full bicone of this half angle, and half that for the cone over an infinite ground plane.

references: Kandoian, Three new antenna types and their applications, Proc. IRE 34(2), 1946
Nail, Designing discone antennas, Electronics 26(8), 1953
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 9.5 for the biconical basis
Low cutoff, VSWR, bandwidth and directivity solved here as a body of revolution (otahub.num.bor), checked against the wire code on a tube, Schelkunoff's bicone and image theory

archetypes.name: Conical monopole
archetypes.summary: A single cone over a ground plane: half a biconical by image theory. Its 50 ohm cutoff, bandwidth and directivity are solved as a body of revolution rather than taken from the quarter-wave rule.

parameters.name: slant length at f_low, in wavelengths

synthesis.notes: SOLVED, tabulated: the slant (from the ideal apex) at which VSWR in 50 ohm first falls to 2 and stays there, from otahub.num.bor - the cone and its image as one solid bicone, half the impedance - on meshes of 24 and 48 segments per slant, extrapolated. 0.2322 at the default 47 degrees, so a quarter wave is 8% LONG there. But the cutoff climbs steeply below about 34 degrees: the cone's impedance rises above 50 ohm and the first near-match, at a fifth of a wavelength, stops reaching VSWR 2 - 0.22 wavelengths at 34 degrees, 0.35 at 32, 0.40 at 30, 0.54 at 20. Extra table nodes at 32, 32.5 and 33 degrees follow that slope.
The feed: the cone truncated where the coax inner conductor meets it, at 2% of the base diameter - the same proportion the discone is solved with.
Spacing between the cone's top face and the ground plane, 0.3 x the top diameter.
height of the truncated cone, top face to base

analysis.notes: Zc = (eta0/2pi)*ln(cot(theta/2)) - exactly half the biconical, because the ground plane supplies the missing half by imaging. Infinite-cone value: a truncated cone oscillates about it with frequency.
Inverted from the impedance formula: 46.96 degrees. Wider cones go below 50 ohm, narrower ones above.
purely from the characteristic impedance mismatch, ignoring the reactive end effect of truncation
forward check: must return f_low

SOLVED, tabulated: f_high/f_low for the continuous band with VSWR under 2 in 50 ohm; 10 means it ran past a decade. The indicative decade holds from 30 to 55 degrees. It fails both ways: 1.2-1.5:1 at 15-20 degrees, where the cone's impedance is too high for 50 ohm, 8.3:1 or more at 25 (the survey ended there), and 1.6:1 at 65, where it is too low. Below 15 degrees there is no 50 ohm band at all.
SOLVED, tabulated: the highest VSWR in 50 ohm between 2 f_low and 10 f_low. 1.39 at the default.

SOLVED, tabulated: peak directivity at f_low, over the infinite ground plane (twice the bicone's). 2.873 at the default. It is higher for narrow cones because their cutoff slant is longer, not because the cone is narrow. The wire-cage fit this replaces was evaluated at a quarter-wave slant and ran 0.7-2.8% above the solid cone even there.

validity: solved for half angles 15-65 degrees; below 15 degrees there is no 50 ohm band
infinite perfect ground plane; a finite one tilts the pattern upward and raises the low-frequency VSWR
solid cone truncated at the stated feed (top 2% of the base diameter, 0.3 x that above the plane); a very different feed moves the band edges
50 ohm reference for every VSWR quoted

known_cases.source: Exactly half this toolkit's biconical spec, which gives 375.50 ohm for the same 5 degree half angle. Two archetypes written independently, agreeing to six figures.
The 50 ohm flare angle, inverted from Zc = (eta0/2pi)*ln(cot(theta/2)): theta = 2*atan(exp(-50*2*pi/eta0)) = 46.96 degrees
Body-of-revolution solve at the default 47 degrees: VSWR = 2 in 50 ohm at a slant of 0.2322 wavelengths, 69.6 mm at 1 GHz - shorter than the quarter wave, 75.0 mm - and directivity 2.8734 there.
Same cone: VSWR under 2 from f_low past 10 f_low, worst 1.392 in band - the decade is real at 47 degrees.

30 degrees: the cone presents 79 ohm, and its first near-match at a fifth of a wavelength stalls at VSWR 2.08, so 50 ohm is reached only at a slant of 0.3975 wavelengths - 59% longer than a quarter wave.
20 degrees, 104 ohm: the 50 ohm band lasts 1.46:1 and the VSWR reaches 2.07 before 10 f_low.

references: Schelkunoff, Theory of antennas of arbitrary size and shape, Proc. IRE 29(9), 1941
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 9.5
Cutoff, bandwidth and directivity solved here as a body of revolution (otahub.num.bor)

mom_directivity_across_band.source: Method of moments, 16-wire biconical cage, doubled for the image

archetypes.name: Rectangular planar monopole
archetypes.summary: Flat rectangular plate over a ground plane, sized by the equivalent-cylinder rule that also fits the disc monopole.

synthesis.notes: Inverted from f_low = 7.2e7/(L + W/2 + p), the equivalent-cylinder rule. The half-width stands in for the equivalent cylinder radius, which is the reading that reproduces this family's disc monopole exactly: a disc of radius r has height 2r and half-width r, giving the same 3r.

analysis.notes: forward check: must return f_low
Well under 0.25: a wide plate resonates lower than a thin wire of the same height, which is the whole point of going planar
Indicative, matching the disc monopole in this family. Rectangular plates are usually a little narrower-band than discs or ellipses because their edges scatter more.
Indicative, as for the disc monopole: roughly dipole-like at the bottom of the band, degrading into higher-order patterns above

validity: the 7.2e7/(L + W/2 + p) rule is empirical, good to roughly 10% on the lower corner
the half-width reading of the equivalent cylinder radius is chosen for consistency with this toolkit's disc monopole; other authors define it differently, so do not mix constants across sources
large ground plane assumed; small ground planes shift the corner and spoil the pattern
bandwidth and directivity figures are indicative

known_cases.source: Square plate at 1.5 GHz: L + L/2 + 1 mm = 48 mm gives L = 31.33 mm. The forward check closing on 1.5 GHz confirms the inversion.
The plate is only 0.157 wavelengths tall where a thin monopole would need 0.25 - the wide plate lowers the resonance by well over a third
Doubling the width for the same cut-off shortens the plate to 23.5 mm: L + W/2 = L + L = 2L = 47 mm

references: Ray, Design aspects of printed monopole antennas for UWB applications, Int. J. Antennas Propag., 2008
Kumar & Ray, Broadband Microstrip Antennas, Artech House 2003, Ch. 8
